lessons.title: Program Structure, Data Types and Variables

before.content_html:
Why Data Types Matter

Every value stored in a Python program has a data type. Choosing the right type is not optional — it determines what you can do with the data. You cannot multiply two strings together arithmetically. You cannot store the word “open” as a Boolean. Getting the type wrong causes errors that are often tricky to diagnose. Python works with five primitive data types you must know, plus structured types for grouping data together.

Key Fact

The five primitive data types are: integer (whole number, e.g. 7 or -3), real (decimal number, e.g. 3.14 — Python calls this float), Boolean (True or False), char (a single character, e.g. 'A'), and string (a sequence of characters, e.g. "hello"). In your exam, use the term real rather than float in written answers.

The Primitive Data Types in Python

An integer stores a whole number. Examples include a player’s score, the number of students in a class, or a person’s age. In Python, you write: age = 16.

A real stores values with a fractional part. Examples include a temperature reading (36.7), a price (12.99), or a percentage (78.5). In Python: temperature = 36.7.

A Boolean holds only one of two values: True or False. Note the capital first letter — Python is case-sensitive. Examples: whether a user is logged in, whether a door sensor is triggered, whether a password matches.

A char stores exactly one symbol. In Python, characters are written in single quotes: 'A', '9', '!'. A string is a sequence of characters — as long or short as needed, including an empty string "". In Python: name = "Priya".

When a user types a number using input(), Python receives it as a string by default. Trying to add two such strings gives concatenation, not arithmetic. For example: "5" + "3" gives "53", not 8. You must convert the input before doing any maths:

age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
year_of_birth = 2026 - age
print(year_of_birth)

Use int() for whole numbers and float() for decimals. This is one of the most common errors in exam answers — always check whether a variable storing user input has been converted to the right type.

Variables and Constants

A variable is a named location in memory whose value can change as the program executes. In Python, you create a variable simply by assigning a value to it: score = 0. Every variable has a name (its identifier), a value, and an implied data type.

A constant is a value that should stay fixed throughout the program. Python does not enforce constants with a keyword, but the convention is to write them in uppercase: MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3. Using a named constant makes maintenance far easier — if you later need to change the maximum to 5, you change it in one place rather than searching through every line of code for the number 3.

Key Fact

Meaningful identifier names make code readable and maintainable. livesRemaining is immediately clear; x or temp is not. Examiners award marks for meaningful identifiers when you write code — single-letter names (except conventional loop counters such as i) will cost marks.

Structured Data Types

Beyond the five primitives, Python supports structured types that group multiple values together. An array (implemented in Python as a list) holds an ordered sequence of values. A record groups related fields of potentially different types — implemented in Python using a dictionary. These are covered in detail in a later lesson.

Writing Readable Code

The specification requires you to write code that is easy for another programmer to read. Four techniques contribute to readability: meaningful identifier names (already covered), correct indentation, useful comments, and consistent use of white space.

In Python, indentation is not optional — it defines code blocks. All statements inside an if, for or function body must be indented by the same amount (usually four spaces). Inconsistent indentation causes an IndentationError.

Hard to read (poor names, no comments, no spacing):

x=int(input(""))
if x>=50:
    print("P")
else:
    print("F")

Easy to read (meaningful names, comment at block level, spacing):

# Check whether a student has passed their exam
score = int(input("Enter exam score: "))

if score >= 50:
    print("Pass")
else:
    print("Fail")

Notice: the comment explains the purpose of the block, not what each individual line does. Over-commenting — adding a comment to every single line — makes code harder to read, not easier. A common mistake in exam answers is writing more comment text than code.

Initialisation and Assignment

Before you can use a variable, you must give it an initial value. This is called initialisation. For example, a score counter should start at zero: score = 0. Running total variables, list index counters and flag variables all need initialisation before a loop begins. Failing to initialise a variable causes a NameError in Python — the program tries to use a name it has never seen before.

When you encounter new code, try to predict its output before you run it. Consider:

total = 0
for i in range(1, 5):
    total = total + i
print(total)

Predict: range(1, 5) produces 1, 2, 3, 4. The loop adds each to total, giving 1, 3, 6, 10. The output is 10. Then run it to verify. This predict-then-run habit is especially useful for tackling “Complete a Trace Table” questions in your exam.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Python has five primitive data types: integer, real (float), Boolean, char and string. Use the term real in written exam answers.
  • Variables hold values that can change; constants (uppercase by convention) hold values that must not change. Both need meaningful identifier names.
  • Readable code uses meaningful identifiers, correct indentation, block-level comments (not per-line) and consistent white space.
before.exam_tip_html: For “Define” questions on data types, be precise: a char holds exactly one character; a string holds a sequence of characters. Examiners penalise vague answers such as “it holds text.” For “Identify” questions about which data type to use, pick the most specific type — if a value is always a whole number, choose integer rather than real. For “Write” questions, always use meaningful identifier names and add one block-level comment — not a comment on every line.

before.content_html:
Operators — The Tools of Calculation

An operator tells Python how to combine or compare values. There are three categories you must know: arithmetic, relational, and logical. Understanding them precisely matters because exam questions often test the output of specific expressions — especially for relational operators where the expected output is True or False, not “yes” or “no”.

Arithmetic Operators

Python supports six arithmetic operators. Four are familiar: + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication), / (real division — the result can be a decimal). The other two are integer division (//) and modulus (%), plus exponentiation (**).

print(17 // 5)    # Integer division: 3 (5 goes into 17 three full times)
print(17 % 5)     # Modulus: 2 (17 = 3*5 + 2, remainder is 2)
print(2 ** 8)     # Exponentiation: 256 (2 to the power of 8)
print(7 / 2)      # Real division: 3.5
Key Fact

The modulus operator (%) returns the remainder after integer division. A classic use is testing whether a number is odd or even: n % 2 == 0 is True if n is even. It also appears in creating circular patterns, validating credit card numbers, and extracting individual digits.

Relational Operators

Relational operators compare two values and always return a Boolean: True or False. This is a common exam error — students write “yes” or “1” when the correct answer is True.

print(10 == 10)   # True
print(10 != 5)    # True
print(3 < 2)      # False
print(5 >= 5)     # True

The six relational operators are: == (equal to), != (not equal to), < (less than), > (greater than), <= (less than or equal to), >= (greater than or equal to). Note that == tests equality; a single = in Python is assignment, not comparison.

This is one of the most common errors in exam answers. If a question asks “what is the output of print(7 > 3)?”, the answer is True (capital T, no quotes). Writing “yes” or “1” is wrong. The result of any comparison in Python is a Boolean value — either True or False.

Logical Operators

Logical operators combine or invert Boolean conditions. Python uses and, or, and not (all lowercase).

age = 17
has_consent = True

if age >= 16 and has_consent:
    print("Eligible for trip")

if age < 13 or age > 65:
    print("Reduced price ticket")

if not has_consent:
    print("Permission required")
Key Fact

and requires all combined conditions to be True. or requires at least one to be True. not inverts: not True gives False. These match the Boolean logic used in search queries, access controls, and input validation throughout real systems.

String Operations

Python has powerful built-in tools for working with strings. The length of a string is found with len(). Indexing retrieves a single character by position, starting at 0. Slicing extracts a section of the string.

name = "Computer"
print(len(name))       # 8
print(name[0])         # "C" (first character, index 0)
print(name[3])         # "p" (index 3)
print(name[0:4])       # "Comp" (index 0 up to but not including 4)

For the string s = "GCSE2026":

  • len(s) → 8
  • s[0] → 'G' (first character)
  • s[-1] → '6' (last character, using negative indexing)
  • s[4:8] → '2026' (characters at positions 4, 5, 6, 7)
  • s[0:4] → 'GCSE' (positions 0, 1, 2, 3)

Remember: Python counts from 0, and the end index in a slice is excluded. So s[0:4] gives characters at positions 0, 1, 2, 3 — not position 4.

Case Conversion and Concatenation

Python provides two methods for changing a string’s case: .upper() returns a version with all letters capitalised; .lower() returns a version with all letters in lowercase. These are useful when comparing user input regardless of how it was typed.

city = "London"
print(city.upper())    # "LONDON"
print(city.lower())    # "london"

# Safe comparison:
response = input("Enter yes or no: ")
if response.lower() == "yes":
    print("Confirmed")

Concatenation joins strings together using +. Only strings can be concatenated — trying to add a string and an integer gives a TypeError. Use str() to convert a number to a string first: "Score: " + str(85).

A school system creates a username from the first letter of a student’s first name plus their full surname, all in lowercase:

first_name = input("First name: ")
surname = input("Surname: ")
username = first_name[0].lower() + surname.lower()
print("Username:", username)

If the student enters “Priya” and “Sharma”, the username becomes “psharma”. This uses indexing ([0]), case conversion (.lower()), and concatenation (+) in a single line.

before.content_html:
Getting Data In and Out

Every useful program exchanges data with the outside world. In Python, print() sends output to the screen and input() reads a value from the keyboard. These are the two most fundamental input/output operations. Beyond the keyboard, programs also read from and write to files — essential for storing data that persists between program runs.

# Basic input and output
name = input("What is your name? ")
age = int(input("How old are you? "))
print("Hello,", name, "- you will be", age + 1, "next year.")

The string passed to input() is the prompt — it appears on screen before the cursor so the user knows what to type. The function always returns a string, so numeric values must be converted with int() or float() before arithmetic can be performed.

CSV Files — Reading Comma-Separated Data

A CSV file (comma-separated values) stores tabular data as plain text. Each line is a row; values within a row are separated by commas. CSV is widely used because every spreadsheet application, database and programming language can read and write it. A student grade file might look like:

name,score,grade
Ali Hassan,78,Pass
Beth Clarke,92,Distinction
Carlos Reyes,54,Pass

Python can read a CSV file using the built-in open() function. When you open a file, you specify a file mode: 'r' for reading, 'w' for writing (overwrites existing content), 'a' for appending (adds to the end).

Reading grades.csv line by line, splitting each line on commas:

with open("grades.csv", "r") as f:
    header = f.readline()    # Skip the header row
    for line in f:
        line = line.strip()  # Remove trailing newline
        fields = line.split(",")
        name = fields[0]
        score = int(fields[1])
        grade = fields[2]
        print(name, "-", score, "(" + grade + ")")

Key steps: (1) open() opens the file in read mode. (2) with ensures the file is closed automatically when the block ends. (3) .readline() reads and discards the header. (4) for line in f processes each remaining row. (5) .strip() removes the invisible \n at the end of each line. (6) .split(",") splits the line into a list of fields.

Creating a new CSV file and writing a header plus data rows:

with open("results.csv", "w") as f:
    f.write("name,score\n")    # Header row
    students = [["Ali", 78], ["Beth", 92], ["Carlos", 54]]
    for student in students:
        f.write(student[0] + "," + str(student[1]) + "\n")

Each row ends with \n (newline character) to move to the next line. Opening in "w" mode overwrites the file if it already exists. Use "a" mode to append new rows without deleting existing data.

Validation Routines

Validation ensures that data entered by a user is reasonable before the program uses it. It does not guarantee the data is correct — a user could enter the wrong date of birth and it might still pass all checks — but it filters out obviously bad data. There are four types of validation check you need to know.

Key Fact

The four validation types are: presence check (is the field empty?), length check (is the data the right number of characters?), range check (is the value within acceptable numeric bounds?), and pattern check (does the data match an expected format?). A password system might use all four.

A presence check confirms that a field has been filled in:

username = input("Enter username: ")
if username == "":
    print("Error: username cannot be empty")

A length check ensures the data is neither too short nor too long:

password = input("Enter password: ")
if len(password) < 8 or len(password) > 20:
    print("Password must be 8 to 20 characters")

A range check tests whether a numeric value is within acceptable bounds:

age = int(input("Enter age: "))
if age < 0 or age > 120:
    print("Age must be between 0 and 120")

Pattern Check

A pattern check verifies that data matches a particular format. This is the fourth validation type and is unique to this specification — it goes beyond simply checking whether a value is present, the right length or in range. A simple pattern check can be written using string operations to test the structure of data.

A simplified UK postcode check: the postcode must be between 6 and 8 characters, contain no spaces for simplicity, and start with letters before digits. A basic pattern check might verify: no spaces, at least 6 characters, and the first two characters are alphabetic:

postcode = input("Enter postcode (no spaces): ").upper()

def is_valid_postcode(code):
    if len(code) < 5 or len(code) > 7:
        return False
    if not code[0].isalpha() or not code[1].isalpha():
        return False
    return True

if is_valid_postcode(postcode):
    print("Valid format")
else:
    print("Invalid postcode format")

Python’s .isalpha() returns True if all characters are alphabetic. .isdigit() returns True if all characters are digits. These built-in methods are enough for a simple pattern check — full regular expressions are not required in your exam.

Key Fact

Validation and authentication are not the same thing. Validation checks that data is in an acceptable format or range — it makes no claim about whether the data is true. Authentication verifies identity by checking credentials against a stored record. A programme may need both: validate the password format first, then check it against the stored value.

Authentication

Authentication checks that a user’s identity matches a stored record. A simple authentication routine compares entered credentials against a list of known users:

# Simple in-memory authentication
users = {"admin": "pass123", "teacher": "gcse2026"}

username = input("Username: ")
password = input("Password: ")

if username in users and users[username] == password:
    print("Access granted")
else:
    print("Invalid credentials")
before.exam_tip_html: For CSV questions, you are expected to know how to open a file with open(), iterate over lines, and split on commas. Always use the with keyword — it automatically closes the file and earns marks in “Write” questions. For validation questions, name the check precisely: presence, length, range, or pattern. Don’t describe them vaguely as “checking the input.” A pattern check is distinct from the other three — it tests the format, not just the value.

before.content_html:
Why Break Code into Subprograms?

As programs grow longer, keeping everything in one flat block of code becomes unmanageable. A subprogram is a named block of code that does one clearly defined job. You call it by name whenever that job needs doing, rather than copying the code every time. Python supports two types of subprogram: procedures and functions. Edexcel is precise about the distinction — confusing them is one of the most penalised errors in exam answers.

Key Fact

A function MUST return a value using return. A procedure does NOT return a value. Both may take parameters. Writing “a function performs a task” without mentioning the return value is an incomplete definition that loses marks.

Procedures in Python

A procedure is defined with def, may take parameters, performs its task, and then simply ends. It does not hand anything back to the line that called it.

def print_greeting(name):
    print("Hello,", name, "- welcome to the system!")

# Calling the procedure
print_greeting("Priya")
print_greeting("Ali")

The procedure executes, produces output, and exits. The calling code receives nothing back. Good uses for procedures: printing a menu, displaying a result, writing a line to a file, sending a notification.

Functions in Python

A function is also defined with def, but it uses return to send a result back. The returned value replaces the function call in the expression where it appears.

def calculate_area(length, width):
    area = length * width
    return area

# Calling the function and using the returned value
room_area = calculate_area(5, 4)
print("Area:", room_area, "square metres")

# The return value can also be used directly in an expression:
if calculate_area(3, 3) > 8:
    print("Room is large enough")

A function that checks if a student has passed (score ≥ 50) and returns a Boolean:

def has_passed(score):
    if score >= 50:
        return True
    else:
        return False

result = has_passed(72)
print(result)    # True

result2 = has_passed(40)
print(result2)   # False

Predict the output: 72 ≥ 50 so the first call returns True. 40 < 50 so the second returns False. The function’s return value is captured in a variable and then printed. This predict-before-run habit is essential for trace table questions.

Parameters

Parameters are the input variables listed in the subprogram’s definition. When you call the subprogram, you pass arguments — the actual values — which are assigned to the parameter names. The order must match: the first argument goes to the first parameter, and so on.

def greet_student(first_name, year_group):
    print("Welcome, Year", year_group, "student", first_name)

greet_student("Beth", 10)   # first_name = "Beth", year_group = 10

Local and Global Variables — Scope

Scope describes which parts of a program can read or change a variable. A local variable is declared inside a def block. It is created when the function is called and destroyed when it returns. Nothing outside the function can access it.

def calculate_tax(price):
    tax_rate = 0.20    # local variable
    tax = price * tax_rate
    return tax

# tax_rate and tax do NOT exist out here
print(calculate_tax(100))   # 20.0

A global variable is declared at module level (outside all functions). It can be read anywhere in the program. To reassign it inside a function, you must use the global keyword; otherwise Python creates a new local variable with the same name instead.

Local variables reduce the risk of bugs. If a global variable called score is shared across ten functions, any one of them could accidentally overwrite it. A bug that corrupts the score could be anywhere in the program — finding it means checking all ten functions. If score is instead a local parameter, only that function can change it. The problem is isolated immediately.

Use global variables only for values that genuinely need to be shared across the whole program — for example, a configuration setting loaded once at start-up, or a game’s running total score that every function needs to update.

Built-in and Library Subprograms

Python comes with many built-in subprograms that are always available: print(), input(), len(), int(), float(), str(), range(). These are functions — most of them return a value. Python also has an extensive standard library of library subprograms that must be imported before use, such as import math and then math.sqrt(25).

Types of Program Error

When a program fails, the error falls into one of three categories. Understanding which type of error you are dealing with determines where to look for the fix.

A syntax error occurs when the code violates the rules of Python. The program will not run at all. Python reports the line number and type of problem. Common causes: missing colon at the end of an if or def line, misspelled keyword, unmatched brackets.

A runtime error occurs during execution. The syntax is correct, so Python starts running the program — but something goes wrong mid-execution. Examples: dividing by zero (ZeroDivisionError), using an index beyond the end of a list (IndexError), trying to convert “hello” to an integer (ValueError).

A logic error is the most difficult to find. The program runs without crashing — but it produces the wrong answer. Examples: using > when the condition should be >=, updating a total inside a loop but printing it inside the loop instead of after it, or initialising an accumulator to 1 instead of 0.

Key Fact

Syntax error: program won’t run at all — Python language rules broken. Runtime error: program starts but crashes during execution — impossible operation attempted. Logic error: program runs to completion but produces the wrong output — the algorithm itself is flawed. Only a logic error can be invisible to Python — the other two produce explicit error messages.

Test Data — Normal, Boundary and Erroneous

Testing requires choosing test data that exercises different parts of the program. Three categories of test data cover the essential cases for any input that must lie within a range.

Normal test data uses typical values well within the valid range. For an age input (0 to 120), normal data might be 25, 45, 67. Boundary test data (also called edge data) tests the extreme limits: for the range 0–120, test 0, 1, 119, and 120. Erroneous test data is deliberately invalid: -1, 121, or “hello” for an age field.

Trace the output of the following function for the call classify(73):

def classify(score):
    if score >= 80:
        return "Distinction"
    elif score >= 60:
        return "Merit"
    else:
        return "Pass"

result = classify(73)
print(result)

Trace: score = 73. Is 73 ≥ 80? No. Is 73 ≥ 60? Yes → return “Merit”. result = “Merit”. Output: Merit. When tracing a function, substitute the argument value for the parameter name and follow each condition in order.
before.exam_tip_html: The most common mark loss in “Write a Subprogram” questions is a function that forgets to include return, or a procedure that accidentally returns a value. Always write the signature first (def name(parameters):), then the body, then return at the end if it is a function. For error-type questions, be precise: a syntax error means Python language rules are broken; a logic error means the algorithm produces wrong results but runs without crashing. “A mistake in the code” is too vague for marks.
